nodes.label: Portuguese Arrival (1498)
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Portuguese arrived on west coast of India from 1498, establishing trading and military stations. Superior military technology (muskets) made them important in regional politics. Travellers like Duarte Barbosa, Domingo Paes and Fernao Nuniz documented Vijayanagara.

nodes.label: European East India Companies
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: English, Dutch and French companies formed to expand commercial activities in the east. Used naval power to control sea trade. Forced Indian traders to work as agents. English emerged dominant.

nodes.label: Black Towns
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Settlements established by European companies within new cities for native traders and craftspersons. 'Blacks' were confined here while 'whites' occupied Fort St. George (Madras) or Fort St. William (Calcutta).

nodes.label: Wajid Ali Shah
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Last Nawab of Awadh whose patronage helped Kathak grow into a major art form. The Lucknow gharana of Kathak developed under his court. Important patron of arts and culture.

nodes.label: Duarte Barbosa
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Portuguese writer who provided detailed account of trade and society in south India after 1500. Part of a wave of European travellers including Jesuit Roberto Nobili and French jeweller Jean-Baptiste Tavernier who documented Indian society.

nodes.label: Presidency Cities
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Bombay, Calcutta and Madras became major colonial cities and capitals of three Presidencies. Originally fishing/weaving villages that grew into commercial and administrative centres under British rule. Each had distinct 'white' and 'black' town segregation.
nodes.chapter_title: Colonial Cities - Urbanisation, Planning and Architecture

nodes.label: Colonial Calcutta
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Capital of British India until 1911. Fort William built 1757. Black Hole incident (1756). Maidan created as military open space. White Town and Black Town segregation. Became centre of commerce, administration and intellectual life. Bengali renaissance began here.
nodes.chapter_title: Colonial Cities - Urbanisation, Planning and Architecture

nodes.label: Fort William (Calcutta)
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Built after Battle of Plassey (1757), massive fort with large open areas around it (Maidan). Symbol of British military power. Earlier Fort William was scene of the Black Hole incident (1756). New fort designed to withstand any future attack.
nodes.chapter_title: Colonial Cities - Urbanisation, Planning and Architecture

nodes.label: Colonial Bombay
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Acquired from Portugal in 1661 as part of Catherine of Braganza's dowry. Developed as major port. Cotton textile mills established from 1850s. Great Indian Peninsular Railway terminus (Victoria Terminus, now CST). Gateway of India built 1911. Massive land reclamation projects.
nodes.chapter_title: Colonial Cities - Urbanisation, Planning and Architecture

nodes.label: Colin Mackenzie
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Engineer, surveyor and cartographer who discovered Hampi ruins in 1800. First Surveyor General of India (1815-1821). Prepared first survey map of Vijayanagara based on memories of Virupaksha temple priests and Pampadevi shrine. Collected local histories for colonial governance.

nodes.label: Presidency Towns
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Calcutta, Bombay and Madras were three major colonial cities (Presidency towns) that grew as centres of trade, administration and military power. Each developed distinct colonial urban character.

nodes.label: Industrial Revolution
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Fundamental transformation in manufacturing, technology, and society that began in Britain around 1760 and spread globally through the 19th century. Shifted production from hand tools and home workshops to machine-based factory production. Transformed economy, society, urbanisation, and eventually global power relations. Began ~1760 in Britain, spread globally through 19c. Shifted production from hand tools and home workshops to machine-based factory production.

nodes.label: Why Britain Led Industrialisation
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Britain had unique advantages: abundant coal and iron deposits, colonial markets and raw materials, a strong navy and merchant fleet, political stability after the Glorious Revolution, a patent system encouraging innovation, agricultural revolution freeing labour, and financial institutions (Bank of England, stock exchanges).

nodes.label: Canal System
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Network of artificial waterways built in Britain from the 1760s to transport heavy goods (coal, iron, pottery) cheaply. The Bridgewater Canal (1761) halved the price of coal in Manchester. By 1830, over 4,000 miles of canals existed. Canals were superseded by railways but were crucial in early industrialisation.

nodes.label: Third Battle of Panipat (1761)
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Decisive battle between Marathas and Ahmad Shah Abdali. Maratha expansion had made other rulers hostile, so they lacked support. Ended Maratha ambitions of replacing Mughal authority at Delhi.

nodes.label: Thomas Munro
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Governor of Madras Presidency who developed the ryotwari system with Alexander Read. Settled revenue directly with individual peasant cultivators without intermediary zamindars. Revenue demand could be revised periodically based on productivity assessment.

nodes.label: History Painting
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Imperial art tradition dramatising British victories in India, like Francis Hayman's 1762 painting of Clive meeting Mir Jafar after Plassey, and numerous paintings of the Battle of Seringapatam against Tipu Sultan.
nodes.chapter_title: The Changing World of Visual Arts

nodes.label: Industrial Revolution's Impact on India
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: British industrialisation devastated India's traditional textile industry. Machine-made British cloth flooded Indian markets while raw cotton was exported from India. Indian artisans and weavers were ruined. India was transformed from a manufacturing economy into a supplier of raw materials and a captive market for British goods.

nodes.label: Rousseau and Social Contract
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Jean Jacques Rousseau proposed government based on social contract between people and representatives. Along with Locke's ideas on individual rights and Montesquieu's separation of powers, shaped revolutionary thought.

nodes.label: Cotton Textile Industry
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: The leading sector of early industrialisation in Britain. Raw cotton imported from colonies (India, Americas) was processed in Lancashire mills. Key inventions: spinning jenny (Hargreaves, 1764), water frame (Arkwright, 1769), spinning mule (Crompton, 1779), power loom (Cartwright, 1785). Production increased enormously while Indian textiles were destroyed.

nodes.label: Spinning Jenny
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Multi-spindle spinning frame invented by James Hargreaves around 1764. Allowed one worker to operate eight spindles simultaneously (later expanded to 120). Dramatically increased yarn production. One of the key inventions that mechanised the cotton textile industry and shifted production from homes to factories.

nodes.label: James Watt
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Scottish inventor and engineer (1736-1819) who transformed the steam engine from a crude pump into an efficient power source. His separate condenser (1769) and rotary motion mechanism revolutionised industry. Partnered with Matthew Boulton for manufacturing. The unit of power 'watt' is named after him.

nodes.label: Richard Arkwright
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: English inventor and entrepreneur (1732-1792) who developed the water frame for spinning cotton (1769) and built the first water-powered cotton mill at Cromford (1771). Often called the 'father of the factory system'. His mills employed hundreds of workers including children. Became one of the wealthiest men in Britain.

nodes.label: Steam Engine
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Thomas Newcomen built an early steam engine for pumping water from mines (1712). James Watt dramatically improved it (1769), making it efficient and versatile. Applied to factories, railways, and ships. Freed industry from dependence on water power and location near rivers. The defining technology of the Industrial Revolution. Newcomen's early mine-pump engine 1712; Watt's separate condenser 1769 made it efficient and rotary. Applied to factories, railways, ships.

nodes.label: EIC Revenue for Textile Purchase
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: After gaining political power in Bengal, the English East India Company no longer imported silver to buy Indian goods. Instead they collected revenues from peasants and zamindars and used this revenue to purchase Indian textiles.
nodes.chapter_title: Weavers, Iron Smelters and Factory Owners

nodes.label: Factory System
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: New mode of production replacing cottage industry and artisan workshops. Workers gathered in large buildings with powered machinery, working fixed hours under supervision. Richard Arkwright's Cromford Mill (1771) was an early example. Enabled mass production, division of labour, and employer control over the work process.

nodes.label: Opium Cultivation in Bengal
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: British forced Bengal peasants to grow opium for export to China through advance system. Peasants lost food crop land. EIC used opium trade to balance Chinese tea purchases. Caused Opium Wars with China. British opium monopoly 1773. Peasants tied to system via mahato (headman) advances. Pykars (travelling traders) offered higher prices from princely states (Central India, Rajasthan) — British tried to suppress as smuggling.

nodes.label: Louis XVI
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Bourbon king who ascended French throne in 1774 at age 20. Found empty treasury due to wars. Called Estates General in 1789 which led to revolution. Executed publicly on 21 January 1793 for treason. Bourbon king, ascended 1774 at age 20. Empty treasury from wars. Called Estates General 5 May 1789. Tried and executed by guillotine 21 January 1793.

nodes.label: Bahadur Shah Zafar II
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Last Mughal emperor, declared leader of the revolt by sepoys who marched from Meerut to Delhi in May 1857. Had no real military power but provided symbolic legitimacy. After suppression, tried and exiled to Rangoon (Myanmar) where he died in 1862. Tried by British military commission and exiled to Rangoon where he died in 1862. Captured at Humayun's Tomb after Delhi fell 20 Sept 1857. Tried by British military commission; deported to Rangoon (Burma) where he died 1862.
nodes.chapter_title: Rebels and the Raj - The Revolt of 1857 and its Representations

nodes.label: Adam Smith
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Scottish economist and philosopher (1723-1790), author of 'An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations' (1776). Argued for free markets, division of labour, and minimal government intervention (laissez-faire). Concept of the 'invisible hand' guiding economic activity. Called the father of modern economics.

nodes.label: Capitalism
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Economic system that emerged alongside industrialisation, based on private ownership of the means of production, wage labour, and production for profit. Adam Smith's 'Wealth of Nations' (1776) provided its theoretical foundation with ideas of free markets and division of labour. Generated unprecedented wealth but also stark inequality.

nodes.label: Kunwar Singh
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Zamindar from Jagdishpur (Bihar) who was nearly 80 years old when he led the rebellion in Bihar. Despite his age, fought effectively against British forces. One of the most notable non-sepoy leaders of the revolt, representing zamindar resentment.
nodes.chapter_title: Rebels and the Raj - The Revolt of 1857 and its Representations

nodes.label: Indigo Plantation System
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: European planters in Bengal forced peasants to grow indigo through advances (dadon) that trapped them in debt cycles. Two systems: nij (planter's own land) and ryoti (peasant's land under contract). Planters used coercion, fraud and intimidation. System collapsed after 1860 rebellion. Two systems: nij (planter own land) and ryoti (peasant contract under dadon advance). Collapsed after Blue Mutiny 1859-60.

nodes.label: Paharias
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Hill people of Rajmahal hills in Bengal-Bihar who lived by shifting cultivation, hunting and gathering forest produce. British initially tried to 'pacify' them, then encouraged Santhals to settle in the plains below, marginalising Paharias from their traditional lands. Rajmahal hills. British policy shifted from pacification to displacement by settling Santhals in the plains below.

nodes.label: Print Culture and French Revolution
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Historians argue print popularised Enlightenment ideas of Voltaire and Rousseau, created culture of dialogue and debate, and literature mocking royalty eroded legitimacy of social order. Prepared conditions for revolution.
nodes.chapter_title: Print Culture and the Modern World

nodes.label: Tipu Sultan's Mural Paintings
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Tipu Sultan resisted British cultural traditions and encouraged local art. Had walls of his Seringapatam palace covered with murals by local artists celebrating his father Haidar Ali's victory at Polilur in 1780.
nodes.chapter_title: The Changing World of Visual Arts

nodes.label: Calcutta Madrasa
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Set up in 1781 to promote study of Arabic, Persian and Islamic law. Warren Hastings supported its establishment as part of the Orientalist approach to education.
nodes.chapter_title: Civilising the Native, Educating the Nation

nodes.label: Industrial Revolution in Britain
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Cotton and iron industries led early industrialisation. Richard Arkwright's cotton mill (1781) introduced new discipline. But even in 1840s, hand labour dominated. New technology adopted slowly and unevenly.

nodes.label: Orientalism
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Scholarly tradition represented by William Jones and Colebrooke who respected ancient Indian cultures, discovered and translated Sanskrit and Persian texts, and believed British should promote Indian rather than Western learning. Sought to promote Indian rather than Western learning; translated Sanskrit and Persian texts into English.
nodes.chapter_title: Civilising the Native, Educating the Nation

nodes.label: William Jones
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Arrived in Calcutta in 1783 as a junior judge. A linguist who studied Sanskrit with pandits, discovered ancient Indian texts on law, philosophy and science. Set up the Asiatic Society of Bengal with Colebrooke.
nodes.chapter_title: Civilising the Native, Educating the Nation

nodes.label: Asiatic Society of Bengal
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Founded by William Jones and Henry Thomas Colebrooke in Calcutta. Started a journal called Asiatick Researches to publish discoveries about ancient Indian heritage and translations.
nodes.chapter_title: Civilising the Native, Educating the Nation

nodes.label: Colonial Portrait Painting
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Life-size oil portraits became popular among both British and Indian elite. Johann Zoffany was one of the most famous visiting European painters. Portraits displayed lavish lifestyles and imperial power.
nodes.chapter_title: The Changing World of Visual Arts

nodes.label: Picturesque Landscape Painting
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Imperial art tradition depicting India as quaint and untamed. Thomas and William Daniell were most famous practitioners, arriving in India in 1785. Their paintings contrasted ancient decaying India with modern British-ruled Calcutta.
nodes.chapter_title: The Changing World of Visual Arts

nodes.label: Lord Cornwallis
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Governor-General who introduced the Permanent Settlement in Bengal (1793). Believed that fixed revenue would encourage zamindars to invest in land improvement. Also introduced the Cornwallis Code separating revenue and judicial administration.

nodes.label: Marylebone Cricket Club
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: MCC founded in 1787 at Lord's cricket ground in London. Became the custodian of cricket's rules and traditions. Revised laws periodically including allowing wider bats and overarm bowling.
nodes.chapter_title: History and Sport: The Story of Cricket

nodes.label: Australian Aborigines
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Indigenous peoples of Australia with over 65,000 years of continuous habitation, making them one of the oldest surviving cultures. Practised a sophisticated hunter-gatherer lifestyle adapted to the Australian environment. After British colonisation from 1788, they suffered land dispossession, massacres, forced removal of children (Stolen Generations), and near-destruction of their cultures.

nodes.label: British Colonisation of Australia
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Britain established a penal colony at Sydney in 1788 under Captain Arthur Phillip. Free settlers followed, particularly after the wool industry developed. Six colonies were established by the 1850s. The indigenous Aboriginal population suffered massive decline from disease, violence, and dispossession. Federation into the Commonwealth of Australia occurred in 1901.

nodes.label: Terra Nullius
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Legal doctrine meaning 'land belonging to nobody', used by the British to justify colonisation of Australia from 1788. Denied Aboriginal land ownership despite over 65,000 years of habitation. Overturned by the Australian High Court in the Mabo judgment (1992), which recognised native title.

nodes.label: Storming of the Bastille
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: On 14 July 1789, about 7,000 citizens stormed the fortress-prison Bastille in Paris, symbol of despotic royal power. Commander killed, prisoners released. Followed by peasant revolts and abolition of feudal system. 14 July 1789, ~7,000 citizens attacked fortress-prison Bastille. Commander killed; symbolic end of despotic power. Triggered peasant revolts and abolition of feudalism.

nodes.label: Declaration of Rights of Man and Citizen
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Established natural and inalienable rights: life, freedom of speech, equality before law. Constitution of 1791 made France a constitutional monarchy but gave voting rights only to propertied men above 25. August 1789. Proclaimed natural and inalienable rights: liberty, property, security, resistance to oppression. Constitution 1791 = constitutional monarchy with voting for propertied men over 25.

nodes.label: Estates General
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Political body with representatives from three estates. Last met in 1614 before Louis XVI called it on 5 May 1789 to pass new taxes. Third estate demanded voting by head not by estate, walked out when refused. Three-estate body. Had not met since 1614. Summoned 5 May 1789 to approve new taxes. Third Estate demanded voting by head, walked out, declared itself National Assembly 17 June, Tennis Court Oath 20 June.

nodes.label: French Revolution
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Began with storming of the Bastille on 14 July 1789. Led to end of monarchy, execution of Louis XVI in 1793, and establishment of a republic. Ideas of liberty, equality and fraternity became its lasting legacy. Storming Bastille 14 July 1789. Execution Louis XVI 21 Jan 1793. Liberty, Equality, Fraternity became lasting legacy. Abolished feudal privileges, declared Rights of Man.

nodes.label: French Revolution and Clothing
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Revolution abolished sumptuary laws. Jacobins called themselves sans-culottes (without knee breeches). Blue-white-red national colours, red cap of liberty, long trousers became symbols of patriotic citizenship and equality.

nodes.label: National Assembly of France
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Third Estate declared itself National Assembly on 20 June 1789 at tennis court in Versailles. Led by Mirabeau and Abbe Sieyes. Swore not to disperse till a constitution limiting monarchy was drafted.

nodes.label: Nationalism in 19th Century Europe
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Emerged as a force bringing sweeping changes, replacing multi-national dynastic empires with nation-states. Driven by shared identity, common history and culture. French Revolution was the first clear expression.
nodes.chapter_title: The Rise of Nationalism in Europe

nodes.label: Three Estates of France
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: French society divided into First Estate (clergy), Second Estate (nobility) both exempt from taxes, and Third Estate (peasants, artisans, merchants, lawyers). Peasants were 90% of population but only Third Estate paid taxes.

nodes.label: Wootz Steel
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Special high-carbon steel produced all over south India, used to make Tipu Sultan's legendary swords. The process fascinated European scientists including Michael Faraday. The technique was completely lost by mid-nineteenth century due to British conquest. Fascinated European scientists including Michael Faraday. Production technique lost by mid-19c after British conquest disrupted Indian smelters.
nodes.chapter_title: Weavers, Iron Smelters and Factory Owners

nodes.label: Benaras Sanskrit College
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Hindu College established in Benaras (Varanasi) in 1791 to encourage study of ancient Sanskrit texts useful for administration of the country.
nodes.chapter_title: Civilising the Native, Educating the Nation

nodes.label: Olympe de Gouges
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Wrote Declaration of Rights of Woman and Citizen in 1791 protesting women's exclusion from basic rights. Criticised Jacobin government for closing women's clubs. Tried for treason and executed in 1793. Wrote Declaration of the Rights of Woman and the Female Citizen (1791) answering the male-only Rights of Man. Criticised Jacobin closure of women's clubs. Guillotined November 1793.

nodes.label: Jacobins
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Political club led by Robespierre, mainly from less prosperous sections - shopkeepers, artisans, servants. Known as sans-culottes (without knee breeches). Stormed Tuileries Palace in August 1792, established republic. Club led by Robespierre, drew from less-prosperous sections (shopkeepers, artisans). Known as sans-culottes. Stormed Tuileries August 1792, established republic September 1792.

nodes.label: Bengal Zamindars under Company
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Under Permanent Settlement, many old zamindari families lost lands at revenue auctions. New purchasers were often urban moneylenders. Zamindars' power limited - could not evict peasants easily. Jotedars (rich peasants) emerged as powerful figures controlling local resources.

nodes.label: Colonial Agrarian Legislation
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Series of laws reshaping Indian agrarian relations: Bengal Regulation (1793), various Tenancy Acts, Deccan Agriculturists' Relief Act (1879). These defined property rights, revenue obligations and debtor-creditor relations in ways that transformed traditional rural society.

nodes.label: Permanent Settlement (1793)
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Introduced by Lord Cornwallis in Bengal in 1793. Fixed revenue demand permanently with zamindars as intermediaries. Zamindars who failed to pay lost lands in auctions. Aimed to create loyal class of landowners. Led to rack-renting of peasants and sub-infeudation. Sunset Law fixed payment deadlines; defaulting zamindars lost lands at auction, often to Calcutta absentee purchasers (urban moneylenders).

nodes.label: Reign of Terror
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Period 1793-94 under Robespierre marked by severe repression. Ex-nobles, clergy, political opponents arrested and guillotined by revolutionary tribunal. Wages and prices fixed, white flour banned, churches shut.

nodes.label: Maximilian Robespierre
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Leader of Jacobins who implemented the Reign of Terror (1793-94) with severe control and punishment. Guillotined opponents, rationed bread, shut churches. Ultimately arrested and guillotined by his own party in July 1794. Led Jacobin Reign of Terror 1793-94. Fixed wages and prices, rationed bread, shut churches. Arrested and guillotined by his own party July 1794.

nodes.label: Abolition of Slavery in French Colonies
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Convention legislated in 1794 to free all slaves in French overseas possessions. Slave trade had linked Europe, Africa and Americas. Napoleon reintroduced slavery. Final abolition in French colonies only in 1848. Convention legislated emancipation 1794 in French colonies. Napoleon reinstated slavery 1802. Final abolition 1848.

nodes.label: Maharaja Ranjit Singh
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Reunited Sikh groups and established capital at Lahore in 1799. Sikh territories extended from the Indus to the Jamuna. Created a powerful kingdom that lasted until British annexation.

nodes.label: Tipu Sultan's Sword
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Made of Wootz steel with incredibly hard and sharp edge. Gold quotations from the Koran were inscribed on the handle. Tipu fought four wars with the British and died fighting in 1799. Tipu died defending Seringapatam in the Fourth Anglo-Mysore War (1799).
nodes.chapter_title: Weavers, Iron Smelters and Factory Owners

nodes.label: Company Paintings
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Paintings produced by local Indian artists for East India Company officials depicting plants, animals, monuments, festivals, trades and castes. Represented Indians as specimens of different communities. Lord Impey + Marquess Wellesley patronised. Famous artists: Sewak Ram, Ishwari Prasad, Ghulam Ali Khan. Water colour with linear perspective + shading. Centres: Kolkata, Chennai, Delhi, Patna, Varanasi, Thanjavur.
nodes.chapter_title: The Changing World of Visual Arts

nodes.label: De-urbanisation in 19th Century
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Many pre-colonial cities like Machilipatnam, Surat and Seringapatam declined as trade routes shifted and colonial policies drained traditional industries. Handloom weavers and artisans were ruined. Population of old trading centres fell while port cities grew.
nodes.chapter_title: Colonial Cities - Urbanisation, Planning and Architecture

nodes.label: Factory System and Discipline
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Factories imposed new work discipline: fixed hours, supervised labour, fines for lateness. Workers resisted through strikes and absenteeism. Women and children exploited in early factories with long hours and low wages.

nodes.label: Francis Buchanan
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Employed by East India Company to survey eastern India in early 19th century. His reports provide detailed accounts of local communities, agriculture and natural resources. Used by historians to understand pre-colonial and early colonial rural society in Bengal and Bihar. Surveyed Mysore 1807; Bengal-Bihar early 19c. Ethnographic + ecological reports extensively used by later historians.

nodes.label: Jotedars
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Rich peasants in Bengal who controlled much of local trade and moneylending. Exercised more effective authority than zamindars over peasants. Resisted zamindars' attempts to increase revenue. Could prevent zamindars from exercising power by lending land to peasants. Actively resisted zamindar authority; held more effective power on the ground than many zamindars.

nodes.label: Serampore Mission
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Christian missionary centre established by William Carey near Calcutta in area under Danish East India Company. Set up printing press in 1800 and college in 1818 to promote moral education.
nodes.chapter_title: Civilising the Native, Educating the Nation

nodes.label: Colonial Urban Planning
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: British imposed new urban visions: wide roads, public buildings, clock towers, parks. Segregation between European and Indian quarters. Improvement Trusts established (Bombay 1898). Plague and fire used as pretexts for demolition and replanning of Indian areas. Bombay Improvement Trust established 1898. Plague and fire used as pretexts for demolition and replanning of Indian quarters.
nodes.chapter_title: Colonial Cities - Urbanisation, Planning and Architecture

nodes.label: American Frontier
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: The moving boundary of European-American settlement westward across North America. The frontier experience shaped American identity, democracy, and individualism (as argued by historian Frederick Jackson Turner). But it came at the cost of indigenous displacement, environmental destruction, and violence.

nodes.label: Manifest Destiny
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: 19th-century ideology asserting that the United States was destined to expand across the North American continent. Justified the displacement of Native Americans and the annexation of Mexican territory. Combined nationalism, racial superiority, and religious mission. Used to legitimise territorial expansion and settler colonialism.

nodes.label: Westward Expansion (USA)
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: The expansion of the United States from the Atlantic coast to the Pacific Ocean during the 19th century. Driven by the ideology of 'Manifest Destiny' -- the belief that American expansion was divinely ordained. Involved the Louisiana Purchase (1803), Mexican-American War, Oregon Trail migration, and California Gold Rush. Resulted in massive displacement of Native Americans.

nodes.label: Napoleon Bonaparte
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Rose to power after Directory's instability. Crowned Emperor in 1804. Conquered much of Europe, introduced uniform laws, metric system, protection of private property. Defeated at Waterloo in 1815. Rose to power after Directory collapse. Crowned Emperor 1804. Conquered most of Europe. Uniform laws, metric system. Defeated at Leipzig 1813 and Waterloo 1815. Died in exile on St. Helena 1821.

nodes.label: Napoleon's Administrative Reforms
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Napoleon introduced Civil Code 1804 abolishing birth-based privileges, establishing equality before law, securing property rights. Simplified administrative divisions, abolished feudal system, improved transport. Initially seen as liberator, later as invader. Civil Code 1804 (Code Napoléon) abolished birth privileges, established equality before law, secured property rights. Metric system, uniform administration. Initially hailed as liberator, later resented as invader.
nodes.chapter_title: The Rise of Nationalism in Europe

nodes.label: Settler Colonialism
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Form of colonialism where settlers permanently occupy and displace indigenous peoples from their lands. Unlike extractive colonialism (which exploited resources and labour), settler colonialism aimed to replace the native population. Occurred in North America, Australia, South Africa, and parts of South America from the 16th century onward.

nodes.label: Urbanisation of London
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: London grew from 1 million (1810) to 6.5 million (1880). Industrialisation drew migrants. Five-six people lived per tenement room. Cholera and typhoid epidemics led to public health reforms and underground railway (1863).

nodes.label: Luddites
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Workers who protested against labour-saving machinery by destroying it, active particularly in 1811-1816 in England. Named after the possibly mythical Ned Ludd. Mainly textile workers (croppers, framework knitters) whose skills were being made obsolete. The government suppressed them harshly with military force and hangings.

nodes.label: Industrial Urbanisation
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Rapid growth of industrial cities like Manchester, Birmingham, Leeds, and Sheffield. Manchester grew from 25,000 (1772) to 300,000 (1850). Cities suffered from overcrowding, pollution, disease (cholera, typhus), lack of sanitation, and child labour. Eventually led to public health reforms and urban planning.

nodes.label: Industrial Working Class
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: New social class of wage labourers in factories, mines, and mills. Worked 14-16 hour days in dangerous conditions for low wages. Women and children formed a large part of the workforce. Workers gradually organised into trade unions and Chartist movement to demand rights. Their conditions inspired socialist thought.

nodes.label: Lord Dalhousie
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Governor-General (1848-1856) who aggressively expanded British territory through Doctrine of Lapse and outright annexation. Annexed Satara, Jhansi, Nagpur, Awadh and Punjab. His policies directly provoked many groups who later joined the 1857 revolt.
nodes.chapter_title: Rebels and the Raj - The Revolt of 1857 and its Representations

nodes.label: Fifth Report (1813)
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Report submitted to British Parliament in 1813 on East India Company's administration in India. Over 1000 pages with appendices. Shaped British views of Indian land revenue. Cited extensively by critics of Company misrule. Perspective influenced by colonial revenue collectors.

nodes.label: Tantia Tope
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Military commander who fought alongside Nana Sahib at Kanpur and later with Rani Lakshmibai. Led guerrilla warfare across Central India after fall of major rebel centres. Betrayed by a former associate, captured and executed by the British in April 1859.
nodes.chapter_title: Rebels and the Raj - The Revolt of 1857 and its Representations

nodes.label: Congress of Vienna 1815
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Met in 1815 after Napoleon's defeat. Hosted by Austrian Chancellor Metternich. Restored conservative monarchies, redrew European boundaries to create buffer states. Sought to undo revolutionary changes and balance power. Hosted by Austrian Chancellor Metternich. Restored conservative monarchies, redrew boundaries to create buffer states (Netherlands, Prussia's Rhine gain). Aimed to undo revolutionary ideals.
nodes.chapter_title: The Rise of Nationalism in Europe

nodes.label: Begum Hazrat Mahal
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Wife of deposed Nawab of Awadh who led the revolt in Lucknow on behalf of her son Birjis Qadr. Organised military resistance against the British. Countered Queen Victoria's proclamation with her own proclamation. Fled to Nepal after defeat.
nodes.chapter_title: Rebels and the Raj - The Revolt of 1857 and its Representations

nodes.label: Hill Stations
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Colonial settlements at high altitudes: Shimla, Darjeeling, Ooty, Mount Abu. Served as summer capitals and sanatoriums. Shimla became summer capital of British India. Designed to replicate English countryside. Reflected racial segregation and colonial health anxieties.
nodes.chapter_title: Colonial Cities - Urbanisation, Planning and Architecture

nodes.label: James Mill on Education
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: James Mill attacked Orientalists, arguing education should teach what was useful and practical rather than pleasing natives. Indians should learn Western science and technical advances, not Oriental poetry and sacred literature.
nodes.chapter_title: Civilising the Native, Educating the Nation

nodes.label: Ryotwari Settlement
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: System introduced in Bombay and Madras Presidencies where revenue was settled directly with individual cultivators (ryots). No intermediary zamindars. Revenue demand could be revised periodically. Devised by Thomas Munro and Alexander Read.

nodes.label: Rammohun Roy and Press Freedom
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Published Sambad Kaumudi in Bengali and Mirat-ul-Akhbar in Persian. Protested Press Regulations of 1823 arguing free press needed for reform. Petitioned against censorship as violation of natural rights. Published Sambad Kaumudi (Bengali) and Mirat-ul-Akhbar (Persian). Protested 1823 Press Regulations, argued free press is a natural right.
nodes.chapter_title: Print Culture and the Modern World

nodes.label: Clothing and Caste in India
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Strict codes governed what different castes could wear. Shanars/Nadars of Travancore forbidden from covering upper bodies. Their struggle to wear cloth on upper body became a movement for dignity and equality.

nodes.label: Mahalwari Settlement
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Revenue system introduced in North-Western Provinces, Punjab and parts of Central India. Revenue settled with village or mahal as a unit. Devised by Holt Mackenzie. Village headman collected and paid revenue on behalf of the entire village community.

nodes.label: Shanar Breast Cloth Movement
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Shanars of Travancore challenged caste prohibition on covering upper body. Converted Shanars began wearing cloth. Upper castes attacked them. British intervened in 1829 allowing converted Christian women to cover upper bodies.

nodes.label: Nana Sahib
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Adopted son of Peshwa Baji Rao II. Led rebellion at Kanpur. Declared himself Peshwa. His claim to the Peshwa's pension had been denied by the British under the Doctrine of Lapse. Fled and disappeared after British recaptured Kanpur.
nodes.chapter_title: Rebels and the Raj - The Revolt of 1857 and its Representations

nodes.label: Trade Unions
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Workers' organisations formed to collectively bargain for wages, hours, and conditions. Initially illegal under the Combination Acts (1799-1800), legalised in 1824. The Grand National Consolidated Trades Union (1834) and later the Trades Union Congress (1868) were milestones. Unions became a major political force and contributed to the Labour movement.

nodes.label: Rani Lakshmibai
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Queen of Jhansi whose state was annexed under Doctrine of Lapse after her husband's death. Joined the revolt in 1857. Fought fiercely, captured Gwalior fort. Died fighting in June 1858. Became an iconic symbol of resistance. Hugh Rose called her 'the best and bravest' of rebel leaders. Died fighting Gwalior 17 June 1858. General Hugh Rose: "here lay the woman who was the only man among the rebels."
nodes.chapter_title: Rebels and the Raj - The Revolt of 1857 and its Representations

nodes.label: Raja Rammohun Roy
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Founded Brahmo Sabha (later Brahmo Samaj) in Calcutta. Campaigned against sati using ancient texts to show it had no sanction. Advocated Western education and women's rights. Sati was banned in 1829 due to his efforts.

nodes.label: Abolition of Sati
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Practice of widows being burnt on husband's funeral pyre was banned in 1829 through efforts of Rammohun Roy. He used ancient texts to prove it had no scriptural sanction, a strategy adopted by later reformers.

nodes.label: Brahmo Samaj
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Reform association formed in 1830, prohibited idolatry and sacrifice, drew upon Upanishads. Led by Rammohun Roy, later by Keshub Chunder Sen. Critically drew upon ideals of Hinduism and Christianity.

nodes.label: Captain Swing Riots
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: From 1830, labourers destroyed 387 threshing machines across southern England, protesting loss of livelihood to mechanisation. Letters signed 'Captain Swing'. Government response severe: 9 hanged, 505 transported to Australia.

nodes.label: Decline of Indian Textiles
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: By the 1830s British cotton cloth flooded Indian markets. By the 1880s two-thirds of cotton clothes worn by Indians were British-made. Thousands of weavers and spinners lost their livelihood and became agricultural labourers or migrated.
nodes.chapter_title: Weavers, Iron Smelters and Factory Owners

nodes.label: Pathshala System
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: William Adam's report in 1830s found over 1 lakh pathshalas in Bengal and Bihar teaching over 20 lakh children. Flexible system with no fixed fees, timetable or examinations. After 1854, government imposed new rules destroying this flexibility. William Adam's 1830s report found ~1 lakh pathshalas in Bengal and Bihar teaching ~20 lakh children. Post-1854 Wood's Despatch eroded this flexibility.
nodes.chapter_title: Civilising the Native, Educating the Nation

nodes.label: Railways
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: George Stephenson's Rocket (1829) proved the viability of steam-powered railways. The Liverpool-Manchester line (1830) was the first intercity passenger railway. Railways transformed transportation, enabled rapid movement of goods and people, created massive demand for iron and coal, and opened up new markets. By 1850, Britain had 6,000 miles of track. Stephenson's Rocket 1829 proved viability. Liverpool-Manchester 1830 first intercity passenger railway. By 1850, Britain had ~6,000 miles of track.

nodes.label: Romantic Nationalism
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Cultural movement using folk songs, poetry, dance to shape national identity. Grimm Brothers collected folk tales. Karol Kurpinski used polkas and polonaises for Polish national struggle. Language became marker of nationality.
nodes.chapter_title: The Rise of Nationalism in Europe

nodes.label: Threshing Machine
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Mechanical device that replaced hand threshing of grain. Its introduction in early 19th century England displaced agricultural labourers, triggering Captain Swing riots. Symbolised conflict between mechanisation and employment.

nodes.label: Trail of Tears
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Forced relocation of approximately 60,000 Native Americans (Cherokee, Creek, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Seminole) from their ancestral lands in the southeastern USA to Indian Territory (Oklahoma) in the 1830s. Thousands died from exposure, disease, and starvation during the march. Resulted from the Indian Removal Act (1830) signed by President Andrew Jackson.

nodes.label: Giuseppe Mazzini
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Italian revolutionary who founded Young Italy and Young Europe. Believed in unitary Italian republic. Inspired nationalists across Europe and India. Metternich described him as 'the most dangerous enemy of our social order'. Italian revolutionary. Founded Young Italy (1831) and Young Europe. Believed in unitary Italian republic. Inspired nationalists across Europe and India. Metternich called him "most dangerous enemy of our social order".
nodes.chapter_title: The Rise of Nationalism in Europe

nodes.label: Frontier Wars
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Armed conflicts between settlers and indigenous peoples on expanding colonial frontiers. In North America, these included King Philip's War (1675), the Indian Wars of the 19th century (including the Battle of Little Bighorn, 1876, and Wounded Knee massacre, 1890). In Australia, the frontier wars (1788-1930s) resulted in the deaths of thousands of Aboriginal people.

nodes.label: Greek War of Independence
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Greeks struggled from 1821 against Ottoman Empire. Supported by Western Europeans inspired by ancient Greek culture. Treaty of Constantinople 1832 recognised Greece as independent. Lord Byron participated and died.
nodes.chapter_title: The Rise of Nationalism in Europe

nodes.label: Reservations / Reserves
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Designated areas where indigenous peoples were confined after being displaced from their traditional lands. In the USA, the reservation system was formalised in the mid-19th century, confining tribes to often marginal lands. In Australia, Aboriginal reserves served a similar purpose. Represented a drastic reduction of indigenous territory and autonomy.

nodes.label: Child Labour in Industrialisation
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Children as young as 5 worked in factories, mines, and chimneys. Factory Acts gradually restricted child labour: 1833 Act banned children under 9 in textile mills, 1842 Mines Act banned women and children underground. Reform was driven by public outcry, parliamentary investigations, and campaigns by humanitarians.

nodes.label: Indentured Labour Migration
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: After slavery abolition, Indian and Chinese workers hired on contracts for Caribbean, Fiji, Mauritius, Malaya plantations. Called 'new system of slavery'. Workers faced deception and harsh conditions. Created Indian diaspora.
nodes.chapter_title: The Making of a Global World

nodes.label: English Education Act 1835
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Made English the medium of instruction for higher education in India and stopped promotion of Oriental institutions like Calcutta Madrasa and Benaras Sanskrit College, which were called 'temples of darkness'.
nodes.chapter_title: Civilising the Native, Educating the Nation

nodes.label: Macaulay's Minute on Education
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Thomas Babington Macaulay argued that Eastern knowledge was inferior, declaring a single shelf of European library worth the whole native literature. Led to the English Education Act of 1835 making English the medium for higher education. Famously declared "a single shelf of a good European library was worth the whole native literature of India and Arabia".
nodes.chapter_title: Civilising the Native, Educating the Nation

nodes.label: Charles Dickens
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: English novelist who depicted hardships of the poor and working class. Oliver Twist (1838) showed life in workhouses. Hard Times (1854) critiqued effects of industrialisation. Serialised in magazines, reaching wide audiences.

nodes.label: James Prinsep
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Officer in the mint of the East India Company who deciphered Brahmi and Kharosthi scripts in the 1830s. Found that most early inscriptions mentioned a king called Piyadassi (Ashoka). This was a breakthrough for early Indian epigraphy.
nodes.chapter_title: Kings, Farmers and Towns - Early States and Economies

nodes.label: Opium Wars
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Two wars between China and Britain (1839-42 and 1856-60) triggered by the opium trade. Britain exported Indian opium to China, creating addiction and draining Chinese silver. China's attempts to ban opium led to war. The Treaty of Nanking (1842) ceded Hong Kong, opened five treaty ports, and imposed extraterritoriality. A humiliating symbol of Western imperialism in China. First Opium War 1839-42; Second 1856-60. Treaty of Nanking ceded Hong Kong, opened 5 treaty ports (Canton, Amoy, Foochow, Ningpo, Shanghai), imposed extraterritoriality. Inaugurated China's "century of humiliation".

nodes.label: Kalighat Paintings
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: New art style developed by village scroll painters (patuas) and potters (kumors) who moved to Calcutta in early 19th century. Used bold non-realistic style with shading for three-dimensional effect. Later depicted social satire and nationalist themes.
nodes.chapter_title: The Changing World of Visual Arts

nodes.label: Serialised Novels and Magazines
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Many 19th century novels first published in instalments in magazines and newspapers. This made them affordable for wider readership. Created suspense and discussion around each episode. Expanded reading public.

nodes.label: Waste Land Rules
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Colonial rules aimed at bringing uncultivated land under cultivation. Grazing lands were taken over and given to individuals. Expansion of cultivation reduced pastures available for pastoral communities.

nodes.label: Treaty of Nanking (1842)
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: First of the 'unequal treaties' ending the First Opium War. China ceded Hong Kong to Britain, opened five ports (Canton, Amoy, Foochow, Ningpo, Shanghai) to foreign trade, paid an indemnity of 21 million silver dollars, and granted most-favoured-nation status. Inaugurated a 'century of humiliation' for China.

nodes.label: Birjis Qadr
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Young son of deposed Nawab Wajid Ali Shah, proclaimed ruler of Awadh during the revolt. Begum Hazrat Mahal, his mother, effectively led the resistance in Lucknow. Eventually fled to Nepal after British recapture. Represented Awadh's resistance to annexation.
nodes.chapter_title: Rebels and the Raj - The Revolt of 1857 and its Representations

nodes.label: Corn Laws
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Laws restricting import of corn to protect British landowners. Abolished under pressure from industrialists and urban dwellers who wanted cheap food. Abolition opened British markets to cheap imported grain.

nodes.label: Corn Laws and Global Food Market
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Abolition of Corn Laws in Britain opened economy to food imports. British agriculture declined, workers migrated. Global food trade expanded as lands cleared in Americas, Russia and Australia to feed Britain.
nodes.chapter_title: The Making of a Global World

nodes.label: Revolutions of 1848
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Liberal revolutions across Europe demanding constitutionalism and national unification. Frankfurt Parliament attempted German unification but was opposed by aristocracy and military. Women attended as observers but denied voting rights. Liberal revolutions across Europe — Paris, Vienna, Berlin, Milan — demanding constitutions and nationalist unification. Frankfurt Parliament attempted German unification; crushed by aristocracy and military.
nodes.chapter_title: The Rise of Nationalism in Europe

nodes.label: Parsee Cricket in Bombay
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: First Indian community to adopt cricket, founding Oriental Cricket Club in 1848. Set up first Indian cricket club. Played matches against Europeans and helped establish cricket in India.
nodes.chapter_title: History and Sport: The Story of Cricket

nodes.label: Cricket in Colonial India
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: First Indian cricket club founded in 1848 by Bombay Parsees. Gymkhana tournaments organised on communal lines - Parsees, Hindus, Muslims, Europeans. Pentangular tournament reflected colonial divide-and-rule politics.
nodes.chapter_title: History and Sport: The Story of Cricket

nodes.label: Doctrine of Lapse
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Policy of Lord Dalhousie refusing to recognise adopted heirs of Indian rulers, annexing their states. Applied to Satara, Jhansi, Nagpur and other states. Major cause of resentment among Indian aristocracy. Nana Sahib and Rani Lakshmibai were directly affected. Applied to Satara 1848, Jaitpur 1849, Sambalpur 1849, Jhansi 1853, Nagpur 1854. Awadh annexed 1856 on separate pretext of misgovernment.
nodes.chapter_title: Rebels and the Raj - The Revolt of 1857 and its Representations

nodes.label: Gold Rush
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Discoveries of gold attracted massive migration and accelerated settler colonialism. The California Gold Rush (1848-55) drew 300,000 migrants and devastated local Native American populations. The Australian gold rushes (1851 onwards) in Victoria and New South Wales similarly attracted immigrants and displaced Aboriginal peoples.

nodes.label: Karl Marx
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: With Friedrich Engels developed theory that capitalist society must be overthrown by workers to create communist society where all property is socially controlled. Argued workers would triumph over capitalists.
nodes.chapter_title: Socialism in Europe and the Russian Revolution

nodes.label: Marianne and Germania
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Female allegorical figures representing France (Marianne) and Germany (Germania). Marianne wore red cap and tricolour. Germania wore oak leaf crown, holding sword. Used in coins, statues, stamps to create national identity.
nodes.chapter_title: The Rise of Nationalism in Europe

nodes.label: 19th Century Globalisation
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Three types of flows shaped world economy: trade in goods, labour migration, and capital movement. Railways, steamships and telegraph enabled global connections. Britain emerged as centre of world trade.
nodes.chapter_title: The Making of a Global World

nodes.label: Bombay Deccan Peasants
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Under ryotwari system, peasants were individually assessed for revenue. Many fell into debt to moneylenders (sahukars/sowcars) due to fluctuating cotton prices and revenue demands. When British courts upheld creditor rights, peasants lost lands through foreclosure.

nodes.label: Cricket and Victorian Values
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Cricket became linked to Victorian culture of fair play, discipline and gentlemanliness. Introduced in schools as physical training. Distinction between 'gentlemen' (amateurs) and 'players' (professionals) reflected class hierarchy.
nodes.chapter_title: History and Sport: The Story of Cricket

nodes.label: Dress Reform Movement
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: 19th century movement against restrictive women's clothing. American Amelia Bloomer designed loose trousers (bloomers). In India, Jnanadanandini Devi popularised sari draping styles that allowed greater mobility.

nodes.label: Gaddi Shepherds
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Pastoral community of Himachal Pradesh with similar seasonal cycle to Bakarwals. Winter in Siwalik hills, summer in Lahul and Spiti. Stopped in villages to reap summer harvest and sow winter crop during migration.

nodes.label: Gujjar Bakarwals
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Great herders of goat and sheep in Jammu and Kashmir. Migrated in 19th century. Moved between Siwalik hills (winter) and Kashmir valley (summer) through Pir Panjal passes in groups called kafilas.

nodes.label: Survival of Handloom Industry
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Despite factory competition, handloom survived for fine-quality work machines could not produce - saris with intricate borders, traditional patterns. Adapted by using fly shuttle and focusing on niche markets.

nodes.label: European Managing Agencies
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Bird Heiglers, Andrew Yule, Jardine Skinner controlled large sector of Indian industries till WWI. Indian financiers provided capital but Europeans made all business decisions. Indians barred from European chambers of commerce.

nodes.label: Pastoral Nomadism in India
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Pastoral communities moved cyclically between summer and winter pastures. Mountain pastoralists (Gujjar Bakarwals, Gaddis, Bhotiyas) moved between high meadows and low hills. Plains pastoralists (Dhangars, Banjaras, Raikas) moved across agricultural regions.

nodes.label: Raikas of Rajasthan
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Combined cultivation with pastoralism in Rajasthan desert. During monsoons, moved to Barmer, Jaisalmer and Jodhpur for grazing. In dry months, moved to agricultural areas of Haryana for stubble grazing.

nodes.label: Taiping Rebellion (1850-1864)
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Massive civil war in southern China led by Hong Xiuquan, who claimed to be the brother of Jesus Christ. Established the Taiping Heavenly Kingdom with radical social reforms (land redistribution, gender equality, banning opium). Resulted in an estimated 20-30 million deaths. Weakened the Qing dynasty but was eventually suppressed with Western help. Led by Hong Xiuquan (claimed to be brother of Jesus). Taiping Heavenly Kingdom: land redistribution, gender equality, banned opium. 20-30M deaths. Suppressed with Western help; weakened Qing.

nodes.label: Victorian Women's Dress
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Women tightly laced in stays and corsets from childhood to create small-waisted figure. Clothing reflected ideal of women as frail, submissive and docile. By 1830s suffrage movement campaigned for dress reform.

nodes.label: Wool Industry (Australia)
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Sheep farming became the economic backbone of colonial Australia from the 1820s. The merino sheep thrived in Australian conditions. Squatters occupied vast tracts of Aboriginal land for grazing. By 1850, Australia was the world's largest wool exporter. The wool industry drove territorial expansion and Aboriginal dispossession.

nodes.label: Commodore Perry's Arrival
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: US Navy Commodore Matthew Perry arrived in Japan with warships in 1853, demanding that Japan open its ports to American trade. The unequal Treaty of Kanagawa (1854) was signed under threat of force. This humiliation exposed Tokugawa weakness and catalysed the movement to overthrow the shogunate and modernise Japan. Arrived Edo Bay 1853 with black warships. Treaty of Kanagawa 1854 under force. Humiliation triggered overthrow of Tokugawa → Meiji Restoration 1868.

nodes.label: Railways and Urbanisation
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: First railway 1853 Bombay-Thane. Railways transformed Indian cities: new railway colonies, station architecture (Victoria Terminus), labour migration. Drained hinterland resources to port cities. Created new nodal towns. Railway workshops became centres of working-class consciousness.
nodes.chapter_title: Colonial Cities - Urbanisation, Planning and Architecture

nodes.label: Bombay as Colonial City
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Bombay grew as major trading port and textile centre. Population explosion created crowded chawls where 70% working people lived. Victoria Terminus built 1878-87 symbolised colonial power. Reclamation projects expanded the city. Originally seven islands joined through reclamation (Back Bay, Mahim-Salsette linked by 1862). Population swelled in chawls: 70% of working people in one-room tenements.

nodes.label: First Cotton Mill in Bombay
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: The first cotton mill in India was set up as a spinning mill in Bombay in 1854. By 1900, over 84 mills operated in Bombay, many established by Parsi and Gujarati businessmen. By 1900, 84 mills operated in Bombay; many established by Parsi and Gujarati businessmen.
nodes.chapter_title: Weavers, Iron Smelters and Factory Owners

nodes.label: Indian Textile Industry in 19th Century
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Indian exports declined as British goods flooded Indian markets. First cotton mill in Bombay 1854, first jute mill in Bengal 1855. Indian industries expanded during WWI when British imports declined.

nodes.label: Wood's Despatch 1854
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Educational despatch issued by Charles Wood emphasising European learning for practical and commercial benefits. Led to establishment of education departments, and universities in Calcutta, Madras and Bombay in 1857. Led to establishment of education departments and universities in Calcutta, Madras and Bombay in 1857.
nodes.chapter_title: Civilising the Native, Educating the Nation

nodes.label: Santhal Community
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Tribal community in Bengal-Bihar region who cleared forests for agriculture under British encouragement. Exploited by moneylenders (dikus) and zamindars. Rose in rebellion (Santhal Hool, 1855-56) under leaders Sidhu and Kanhu. Carved out separate Santhal Pargana district. Santhal Hool (1855-56) led by brothers Sidhu and Kanhu against dikus (outsider moneylenders and zamindars); Santhal Parganas district carved out in response.

nodes.label: Annexation of Awadh (1856)
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Governor-General Dalhousie annexed Awadh on grounds of alleged misgovernment of Nawab Wajid Ali Shah. Many sepoys were from Awadh and their families suffered under new revenue arrangements. Taluqdars lost land and power. Massive resentment contributed to revolt.
nodes.chapter_title: Rebels and the Raj - The Revolt of 1857 and its Representations

nodes.label: Ishwarchandra Vidyasagar
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Used ancient texts to argue widows could remarry. A law permitting widow remarriage was passed in 1856. Set up schools for girls in Calcutta. Faced boycott from conservatives for his reformist views. Set up schools for girls in Calcutta. Faced boycott by conservative Hindu society for his reform work.

nodes.label: Sepoy Grievances
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Multiple causes: General Service Enlistment Act (1856) requiring overseas service; low pay compared to British soldiers; racial discrimination; fears of forced conversion to Christianity. Bengal Army heavily recruited from upper-caste Hindus whose status was being undermined. Pay data: infantry sepoy Rs 7/month, cavalry sawar Rs 27/month gross (after own uniform + food + mount upkeep = Rs 1-2 net). Racial discrimination from English officers. 47th Regt 1824 Burma refusal was earliest mutiny (disbanded). Crossing sea = caste loss. Afghan war (1839-42) affected caste purity.
nodes.chapter_title: Rebels and the Raj - The Revolt of 1857 and its Representations

nodes.label: Widow Remarriage Act 1856
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Law passed in 1856 permitting widow remarriage, largely through efforts of Ishwarchandra Vidyasagar. Movement spread to Telugu areas under Veerasalingam Pantulu and to north under Dayanand Saraswati.

nodes.label: Censorship in Colonial India
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: After 1857, British tightened press control. Seditious Materials Act and Vernacular Press Act used to suppress nationalist publications. Despite restrictions, Indian press played crucial role in building anti-colonial consciousness.
nodes.chapter_title: Print Culture and the Modern World

nodes.label: Civilian Participation in 1857
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Not merely a sepoy mutiny but a popular rebellion. Peasants, artisans, small zamindars joined. Awadh saw massive civilian support. Dispossessed taluqdars rallied followers. Rural poor attacked moneylenders and new landlords. Urban poor targeted symbols of colonial authority. Oudh had ~75,000 men in Bengal army. 14,000 sepoy petitions about revenue hardships. Taluqdars lost lands after Awadh annexation (~21,000 estates confiscated). Peasant + artisan + clergy alliance.
nodes.chapter_title: Rebels and the Raj - The Revolt of 1857 and its Representations

nodes.label: Siege of Delhi (1857)
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: After sepoys captured Delhi in May 1857, British forces besieged the city for months. Delhi recaptured in September 1857 with massive violence. Bahadur Shah Zafar tried and exiled. British reprisals included executions, confiscations and destruction.
nodes.chapter_title: Rebels and the Raj - The Revolt of 1857 and its Representations

nodes.label: Greased Cartridges Issue
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Rumour that new Enfield rifle cartridges were greased with cow and pig fat, offensive to both Hindu and Muslim sepoys who had to bite them open. Immediate trigger for the revolt. Reflected deeper anxieties about British interference with religious practices and caste.
nodes.chapter_title: Rebels and the Raj - The Revolt of 1857 and its Representations

nodes.label: Mangal Pandey
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Sepoy of 34th Native Infantry who attacked British officers at Barrackpore in March 1857 over greased cartridges issue. Hanged on 8 April 1857. His action predated the main outbreak at Meerut in May. Became a symbol of the revolt. 34th Native Infantry at Barrackpore. Attacked British officers March 1857 over greased cartridges. Hanged 8 April 1857. 19th Native Infantry at Berhampur refused Enfield cartridges in March 1857 — disbanded. Mangal Pandey (34th NI Barrackpore) fired at Sergeant Major next; overpowered, hanged April 8.
nodes.chapter_title: Rebels and the Raj - The Revolt of 1857 and its Representations

nodes.label: Revolt of 1857
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Major uprising against British East India Company beginning May 1857. Started with sepoy mutiny at Meerut, spread across North India. Rebels captured Delhi, restored Mughal emperor Bahadur Shah Zafar as leader. Suppressed by 1858 with severe repression. Led to end of Company rule and direct Crown control. Started at Meerut 10 May 1857; sepoys marched to Delhi, declared BSZ emperor. Spread across Lucknow, Kanpur, Jhansi, Bareilly, Arrah. Suppressed by mid-1858. Meerut sepoys reached Delhi 11 May 1857, crossing the Jamuna. Half of EIC's 2,32,224 sepoys opted out. Bengal + Bombay + Central + Western India in revolt; Madras army remained loyal; Punjab + South largely quiet.
nodes.chapter_title: Rebels and the Raj - The Revolt of 1857 and its Representations

nodes.label: Aftermath of 1857 Revolt
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Government of India Act 1858 transferred power from Company to Crown. Queen Victoria's Proclamation (1858) promised religious tolerance, respect for rights of princes. British Indian Army reorganised to reduce proportion of upper-caste Hindus. Policy of divide and rule adopted. Government of India Act 1858 transferred power to Crown. Army reorganised: reduced upper-caste Hindu proportion in Bengal Army; recruited more Punjabis and Gurkhas. Divide-and-rule policy formalised.
nodes.chapter_title: Rebels and the Raj - The Revolt of 1857 and its Representations

nodes.label: Queen Victoria's Proclamation (1858)
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Issued November 1858 announcing direct Crown rule. Promised: religious non-interference, respect for rights of Indian princes, equal treatment of subjects regardless of race or creed. Became a charter of rights cited by Indian nationalists in later decades.
nodes.chapter_title: Rebels and the Raj - The Revolt of 1857 and its Representations

nodes.label: Foreign Companies in India
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Foreign companies set up production in India for cheap labour - wages far lower than in developed countries, longer hours, fewer expenses on worker housing. Cost-cutting through lower safety measures. UC plant in Bhopal had far lower safety standards than its US plant in West Virginia.

nodes.label: Rashsundari Devi
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Born in West Bengal around 1800, she wrote Amar Jiban at age 60 -- the first known autobiography by an Indian woman. She secretly taught herself to read and write after marriage, despite the belief that literate women would bring bad luck to their husbands.

nodes.label: Railways Under British Rule
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Introduced in 1850, considered one of the most important British contributions. Had dual impact: enabled long-distance travel breaking geographical and cultural barriers, but also fostered commercialisation of Indian agriculture which harmed village self-sufficiency. Benefits rarely accrued to Indians.
nodes.chapter_title: Indian Economy on the Eve of Independence

nodes.label: Jute Industry
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: India largest producer of raw jute. Mills mostly in West Bengal (Hugli basin). Started 1855. Products: gunny bags, carpets, decoratives. Facing competition from synthetic packaging. Government promotes jute use.

nodes.label: Indigo Rebellion (Blue Mutiny, 1859-60)
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Bengal peasant uprising against oppressive indigo plantation system. Ryots refused to grow indigo. Dinabandhu Mitra's play 'Nil Darpan' (1860) dramatised planter brutality. Government-appointed Indigo Commission led to decline of Bengal indigo. Digambar + Bishnu Biswas led first organised refusal at Govindpur (Nadia) Sept 1859. Lt Gov J.B. Grant: "the root of the question is the struggle to make the raiyats grow indigo plant, without paying them the price of it." Rent strikes, legal action. Complete Hindu-Muslim peasant unity. Factories closed by end 1860.

nodes.label: Sidhu and Kanhu Murmu
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Santhal brothers who led the Santhal Hool (1855-56) in Bengal-Bihar against British officials, zamindars, and moneylenders. Promised divine sanction; mobilised tens of thousands. Brutally suppressed; Santhal Parganas district formed in 1856.

nodes.label: Dietrich Brandis
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: German forester invited by British as first Inspector General of Forests in India (1864). Set up Indian Forest Service and formulated Indian Forest Act of 1865 — framework for scientific forestry and commercial timber extraction.

nodes.label: Indian Forest Act (1865, amd. 1878, 1927)
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Enacted 1865, amended 1878 and 1927. 1878 Act divided forests into reserved, protected, and village forests. Villagers barred from reserved forests; customary use of fuel, fodder, mahua, tendu leaves criminalised. Triggered numerous tribal rebellions.

nodes.label: Scientific Forestry
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Colonial forestry model promoted by Brandis. Natural mixed forests replaced with single-species plantations (teak, sal, deodar, poplar) in straight rows for timber yield. Forest officials surveyed and planned rotational cutting and replanting.

nodes.label: Criminal Tribes Act (1871)
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Classified many nomadic communities (pastoralists, traders, craftsmen) as "criminal by birth". Required notified village settlement, restricted movement, police surveillance. Affected Korava, Karacha, Yerukula and other Madras Presidency groups.

nodes.label: Ban on Shifting Cultivation
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Swidden agriculture (jhum, podu, dhya, bewar, kumri) banned by colonial forest department because it prevented continuous timber growth and made tax collection difficult. Displaced many adivasi communities; fuel for rebellions.

nodes.label: Dhangars
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Pastoral community of Maharashtra, ~467,000 in early 20c. Shepherds, blanket weavers, buffalo herders. Seasonal movement between Deccan plateau (monsoon) and Konkan (post-harvest). Fed on stubble, manured Konkani peasant fields in exchange for rice.

nodes.label: Opium–Tea Triangular Trade
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: British balanced tea imports from China (financed by silver outflow) by smuggling Bengal opium into China. Triangle: Bengal opium → China; China tea → Britain; Britain manufactures → India. Financed EIC tea trade; created Chinese addiction crisis.

nodes.label: Enclosure Acts (Britain)
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Between 1750-1850, British Parliament passed 4,000 Acts enclosing 6 million acres of common land. Late-18c enclosures (vs 16c wool enclosures) were for grain. Landlords displaced poor commoners; set stage for Captain Swing riots. Displaced rural poor migrated to industrial towns, providing factory labour — direct feed into the Industrial Revolution's workforce.

nodes.label: Open Fields and Commons
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Pre-enclosure English rural system. Villagers cultivated strips allocated annually; commons used for grazing, fuelwood, fruit, fishing, hunting. Sustained poor. Swept away by enclosures after 1750.

nodes.label: Cyrus McCormick's Reaper (1831)
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Mechanical reaper invented 1831 in USA. One machine cut as much in a day as 5 men with cradles / 16 men with sickles. Transformed Great Plains wheat harvest; by 20c combined harvesters cut 500 acres in 2 weeks.

nodes.label: USA Great Plains Wheat (Bread Basket)
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Great Plains wheat expansion 1860s-1920s. 45M acres (1910) → 74M acres (1919). Wheat barons controlled 2,000-3,000 acre farms. Steam tractors + combined harvesters. Fed WWI Europe. Later: Dust Bowl 1930s.

nodes.label: Maasai Pastoralists (East Africa)
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: East African cattle herders (Kenya+Tanzania). 1885 Anglo-German border split Maasailand; colonial grazing reserves took best lands. Lost 60% of pre-colonial grazing. Serengeti + Maasai Mara game reserves excluded pastoralists. 1933-34 drought killed over half their cattle.

nodes.label: Dutch Colonial Forestry (Java)
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Dutch imposed forest laws in Java from 19c for teak (shipbuilding, railway sleepers). Blandongdiensten system: villagers given rent exemptions in exchange for free labour cutting and hauling teak. Kalangs (skilled forest cutters) co-opted. Surontiko Samin led 1890s tax resistance.

nodes.label: Commissioner Lin Zexu
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Qing Special Commissioner at Canton 1839. Arrested 1,600 opium traders, confiscated 11,000 lbs opium, burnt 20,000 crates. Wrote "Letter of Advice to Queen Victoria" condemning the opium trade. His closure of Canton triggered First Opium War (1839-42).

nodes.label: Gothic + Neo-Classical Colonial Architecture
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Imposing British-era civic buildings: Victoria Terminus (Bombay, Venetian Gothic 1878-87), High Courts, universities, churches, railway stations. Asserted imperial authority. Prelude to Indo-Saracenic. Also called Indo-Gothic or Victorian style. Thinner walls than Indo-Islamic, pointed arches, large windows. Cruciform church plan. Steel + iron + poured concrete. Examples: Victoria Terminus (VT/CST) Bombay, High Courts, St Paul's Cathedral Kolkata.

nodes.label: Indo-Saracenic Architecture
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Late-19c blend of Hindu/Islamic/European elements. Examples: Gateway of India (Bombay 1911), Madras Law Courts, Mysore Palace (Henry Irwin). Imperial assertiveness with cultural accommodation. Hybrid of Hindu/Islamic/European. Used for Indian princely palaces too — Mysore Palace (Henry Irwin). Gateway of India Mumbai (1924). Madras High Court.

nodes.label: Proto-Industrialisation
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Pre-factory production system where merchants gave advances to rural producers. Large-scale production for international market existed before factories. Challenges view of a sudden factory revolution.

nodes.label: Indian Industrialists (19c)
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Dwarkanath Tagore (Bengal, 1830s), Dinshaw Petit, Jamsetjee Nusserwanjee Tata (Bombay cotton, later TISCO 1912), Seth Hukumchand, G.D. Birla. Rose from trading communities — Marwaris, Parsis, Chettiars, Gujaratis. Barred from European chambers of commerce.

nodes.label: Chawls of Bombay
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Multi-storeyed tenements from 1860s in "native" Bombay. One-room units housed 4-5 people, no private toilets. 90% of mill workers lived in Girangaon chawls, walking distance to mills.

nodes.label: Bombay Land Reclamation
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Seven islands of Bombay joined via reclamation: Back Bay, Mahim-Salsette linkage completed by 1862; Marine Drive later. Transformed geography and enabled chawl + railway expansion.

nodes.label: Indian Textile Trade (pre-1750)
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Before 1750, India was world's largest cotton textile producer. Extensively traded to SE Asia, West + Central Asia, Europe. European companies bought Indian textiles (muslin, calico, chintz) and re-sold at large profits.
nodes.chapter_title: Weavers Iron Smelters and Factory Owners

nodes.label: Muslin
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Term from Mosul (Iraq) where Europeans first saw fine Indian cotton via Arab traders. Came to mean any finely woven cloth. Dacca mulmul celebrated.

nodes.label: Calico
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Derived from Calicut (Kerala coast) where Portuguese first landed (1498). Became generic European term for Indian cotton textiles in trade.

nodes.label: Chintz
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: From Hindi chhint — cotton printed with small flowery designs. From 1680s a craze in England and Europe for texture and relative cheapness. Prompted Calico Act 1720.

nodes.label: Calico Act (1720)
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: British Parliament banned use of printed cotton (chintz) in England to protect English wool and silk industries from Indian textile competition. Early protectionist law against Indian textiles.

nodes.label: Dacca Textile Centre
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Foremost 18c East Bengal textile city, famous for mulmul and jamdani. Weaving industry devastated by British manufactured imports from 1830s — population fell sharply, weavers displaced.

nodes.label: Haussmannisation of Paris
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Baron Haussmann rebuilt Paris 1860s: wide boulevards, parks, open spaces. Destroyed old working-class neighbourhoods. Goal: beautification + prevention of barricade-based revolts.

nodes.label: London Underground (1863)
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: World's first underground railway opened in London 1863. Initially distrusted; expanded with city growth. Shaped London's suburban development pattern.

nodes.label: London Urbanisation Scale
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: London grew from 1M (1810) to 6.5M (1880). Industrial-era migration; 5-6 people per tenement room. Cholera + typhoid drove public-health reform, underground railway (1863), later garden cities.

nodes.label: Jyotirao Phule (early reform)
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Maharashtrian reformer (1827-1890). Set up first girls' school in Pune 1848 with wife Savitribai. Attacked Brahmanical caste hierarchy. Later founded Satyashodhak Samaj (1873) and wrote Gulamgiri (1873) linking caste oppression to American slavery.

nodes.label: Savitribai Phule
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: First Indian woman teacher (1831-1897). With husband Jyotirao Phule set up India's first girls' school in Pune 1848. Wrote poetry on social reform. Faced abuse from upper castes on her way to teach.

nodes.label: Printing in India (pre-1857)
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Portuguese missionaries brought printing to Goa 1550s. First Tamil book printed at Cochin 1579. First Hindi print 1805. Missionaries printed scriptures in Indian languages. First Bengali newspaper Samachar Darpan 1818 (Serampore). Enabled Bengal Renaissance debates.
nodes.chapter_title: Print Culture and the Modern World

nodes.label: Early Indian Novel
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: First modern Indian novels mid-19c. Bankim Chandra's Durgeshnandini 1865 (Bengali), Srinivas Das Pariksha Guru 1882 (Hindi), Chandu Menon Indulekha 1889 (Malayalam). Created a new literary public in regional languages.

nodes.label: Raja Ravi Varma
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Travancore royal (1848-1906). Mastered Western oil technique but painted Ramayana/Mahabharata scenes. Set up mass-production press near Bombay for cheap colour prints that circulated across India — mother-goddess iconography and Hindu epics became visually standardised.
nodes.chapter_title: The Changing World of Visual Arts

nodes.label: Rise of the Novel (Europe)
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: 18c European novel. Defoe's Robinson Crusoe 1719, Richardson's Pamela 1740. Middle-class reading public. Explored individual choice + everyday life.

nodes.label: Gutenberg Print Revolution
nodes.subject: history
