nodes.detail: Johann Gutenberg (Strasbourg) devised movable-type press ~1448. First book: Bible. By 1500 Europe had printed ~20M copies. Knowledge shifted from handcopied manuscripts to mass production. Context for Reformation, later Enlightenment and French Revolution.
nodes.chapter_title: Print Culture and the Modern World

nodes.label: Battle of Plassey (1757)
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: 23 June 1757. Robert Clive defeated Nawab Siraj-ud-daula of Bengal through bribery of commander Mir Jafar. Marked beginning of effective British political control in India. Mir Jafar installed as puppet Nawab.

nodes.label: Battle of Buxar (1764)
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: 22 October 1764. Hector Munro defeated combined forces of Mir Qasim (Bengal), Shuja-ud-daula (Awadh), and Mughal emperor Shah Alam II. Decisive battle that confirmed British supremacy in Bengal; consolidated conquest begun at Plassey.

nodes.label: Treaty of Allahabad (1765)
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: After Buxar. Shah Alam II granted EIC the Diwani (right to collect revenue) of Bengal, Bihar, Orissa. EIC became the de facto fiscal ruler. Awadh returned to Shuja-ud-daula on indemnity payment; became buffer state.

nodes.label: Diwani of Bengal (1765)
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: EIC's right to collect revenue from Bengal, Bihar, Orissa after Treaty of Allahabad. Dual government under Hastings (nominal Nawab + actual EIC control) until 1772 when EIC took direct control.

nodes.label: Siraj-ud-daula
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Last independent Nawab of Bengal (1756-57). Attacked Calcutta 1756 (Black Hole). Defeated at Plassey 1757 by Clive via Mir Jafar's betrayal. Killed soon after.

nodes.label: Mir Jafar
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Bengal military commander who betrayed Siraj at Plassey. Installed as puppet Nawab 1757-60, restored 1763-65. EIC extracted vast wealth through him — 'the Plassey plunder'.

nodes.label: Mir Qasim
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Nawab of Bengal 1760-63. Installed by EIC replacing Mir Jafar, but resisted Company privileges. Fled to Awadh after defeat; fought at Buxar 1764. Died in obscurity.

nodes.label: Robert Clive
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: EIC military commander and governor of Bengal (1757-60, 1765-67). Won Plassey 1757; reorganised revenue administration through Dual Government. Later tried for corruption in Britain.

nodes.label: Warren Hastings
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: First Governor-General of Bengal (1772-1785). Abolished Dual Government. Established civil and criminal courts. Patronised Oriental learning (Calcutta Madrasa 1781). Impeached in Britain on return.

nodes.label: Regulating Act (1773)
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: First British parliamentary intervention in EIC affairs. Created post of Governor-General of Bengal (Hastings first). Established Supreme Court at Calcutta 1774. Brought EIC under parliamentary control.

nodes.label: Pitt's India Act (1784)
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Established Board of Control in London alongside EIC Court of Directors — dual system for governing Indian affairs. Made Governor-General directly accountable to Parliament. Affirmed Company political role.

nodes.label: Charter Act (1813)
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Ended EIC monopoly on Indian trade (except tea and China trade). Allowed Christian missionaries to operate. Imposed on EIC obligation to spend Rs 1 lakh on Indian education annually (origin of colonial education debate).

nodes.label: Charter Act (1833)
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Ended EIC as commercial body — made it purely administrative. Governor-General of Bengal renamed Governor-General of India. First Indian Law Commission (Macaulay) — produced Indian Penal Code draft 1837.

nodes.label: Charter Act (1853)
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Last of the Charter Acts. Introduced competitive exams for ICS. Separated legislative from executive functions of Governor-General's Council — beginning of Indian legislature.

nodes.label: Lord Wellesley
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Governor-General 1798-1805. Architect of Subsidiary Alliance system. Defeated Tipu Sultan (1799), Marathas (2nd Anglo-Maratha War). Massively expanded British territory; recalled for excessive aggression.

nodes.label: Subsidiary Alliance (Wellesley)
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Wellesley's system (from 1798): Indian ruler paid for British troops stationed in territory, accepted British Resident, forfeited independent foreign relations. States joined: Hyderabad (1798 first), Awadh (1801), Mysore (post-1799), Marathas in stages.

nodes.label: Haidar Ali
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Mysore ruler (1761-1782). Modernised army with French help. Fought 1st and 2nd Anglo-Mysore Wars. Expanded Mysore into major south-Indian power. Father of Tipu Sultan. Polilur victory 1780 celebrated in Tipu's palace murals.

nodes.label: Tipu Sultan
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Ruler of Mysore 1782-99, 'Tiger of Mysore'. Modernised army (rockets), sent embassies to France and Ottomans. Fought 3rd + 4th Anglo-Mysore Wars. Died defending Seringapatam 1799. Introduced commercial treaties, land revenue reform.

nodes.label: Anglo-Mysore Wars (4, 1767-1799)
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Four wars between EIC and Mysore. 1st (1767-69): Treaty of Madras. 2nd (1780-84): Haidar vs British; Treaty of Mangalore. 3rd (1790-92): Tipu ceded half his territory. 4th (1799): Tipu killed at Seringapatam; Mysore annexed (partly).

nodes.label: Anglo-Maratha Wars (3, 1775-1818)
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: 1st (1775-82): Treaty of Salbai. 2nd (1803-05): Wellesley vs Sindhia/Bhonsle/Holkar; EIC gains Delhi-Agra region. 3rd (1817-18): Peshwa Baji Rao II defeated; Pune annexed 1818 — end of Maratha power.

nodes.label: First Anglo-Sikh War (1845-46)
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: After Ranjit Singh's death 1839, Sikh succession crisis. British provoked war; defeated Sikh army at Mudki, Ferozeshah, Sobraon. Treaty of Lahore 1846: Sikhs lost Kashmir (sold to Dogra Gulab Singh) and paid indemnity.

nodes.label: Second Anglo-Sikh War (1848-49) + Punjab Annexation
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Triggered by Multan revolt 1848. Battles of Chillianwala, Gujrat 1849. Dalhousie annexed Punjab March 1849 — completed British conquest up to Afghan frontier. Last major Indian military state absorbed.

nodes.label: First Anglo-Afghan War (1839-42)
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: British invaded Afghanistan to place Shah Shuja on throne (countering perceived Russian threat — 'Great Game'). Kabul occupied 1839 then disastrous retreat 1842; only one European survivor reached Jalalabad. Shuja assassinated. Marked end of British aggressive forward policy briefly.

nodes.label: Lord William Bentinck
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Governor-General 1828-35. Reform-minded: abolished sati 1829, suppressed thuggee (1830s via Sleeman), Macaulay's Minute and English Education Act 1835 during his tenure. Revised land settlements in NW Provinces.

nodes.label: General Service Enlistment Act (1856)
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Required new sepoy recruits to serve overseas if ordered. Violated Hindu orthodoxy (crossing kala pani = loss of caste). One of the major grievances underlying the 1857 revolt.

nodes.label: Suppression of Thuggee
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: William Sleeman's campaign 1830s: organised the Thuggee and Dacoity Department. Prosecuted over 3,000 'thugs'. Mix of genuine suppression, orientalist stereotyping, and colonial knowledge production about criminal castes.

nodes.label: Western-vs-Indian Dress Debate
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: 19c Indian elites debated adoption of Western dress. Bengali bhadralok wore chapkan (long coat). Parsis adopted Western suits. Nationalists debated: Tagore experimented with hybrid styles; Vivekananda wore orange robes abroad.

nodes.label: Origins of Cricket (England)
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Evolved from stick-and-ball games ~500 years ago. First Laws of Cricket 1744 (22-yard pitch, 22-inch stumps). World's first club at Hambledon 1760s. MCC (Marylebone Cricket Club) at Lord's 1787 became custodian of laws.
nodes.chapter_title: History and Sport The Story of Cricket

nodes.label: Sumptuary Laws (pre-Revolution France)
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: 1294-1789 French dress codes by class: only royalty wore ermine, silk, velvet, brocade. Swept away by the Revolution — sans-culottes (no knee breeches), long trousers, red liberty cap, tricolour.

nodes.label: Agricultural Revolution (Britain)
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: 18c British farming transformation: crop rotation (turnip + clover), selective livestock breeding, Jethro Tull's seed drill, enclosures. Food surplus freed labour for industrial employment.

nodes.label: Coal and Iron Industries
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Darby's coke-smelting 1709; Cort's puddling process 1784 revolutionised iron production. Coal powered steam engines and heated furnaces. Underpinned railway construction, shipbuilding, machinery.

nodes.label: Qing Dynasty (1644-1912)
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Manchu dynasty, last imperial dynasty of China. Zenith under Kangxi + Qianlong. From 19c: Opium Wars, Taiping, Boxer Rebellion. Failed to modernise adequately; overthrown 1911.

nodes.label: Tokugawa Shogunate (1603-1868)
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Military government ruling Japan. Rigid social hierarchy (samurai/farmers/artisans/merchants). Sakoku isolation limited foreign contact. Internal tensions + Perry's 1853 arrival led to collapse.

nodes.label: Samurai
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Warrior class of feudal Japan serving daimyo lords. Bushido code: loyalty, martial arts, self-discipline. Many became bureaucrats during Tokugawa peace. Meiji Restoration abolished their special status — though many samurai led the modernisation effort.

nodes.label: Meiji Restoration (1868)
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Overthrow of Tokugawa + restoration of imperial rule under Emperor Meiji 1868. Young samurai from Satsuma + Choshu domains led. Slogan 'Enrich the Country, Strengthen the Military' (fukoku kyohei). Launched rapid modernisation catching up with the West.

nodes.label: European Colonisation of Americas
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Begins with Columbus 1492. Spanish/Portuguese/English/French/Dutch colonised. Spanish conquered Aztec + Inca. English coastal colonies became USA. Disease, enslavement, cultural destruction of indigenous peoples.

nodes.label: Native Americans
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Indigenous peoples of N. America, 15,000+ years before European contact. Iroquois, Sioux, Pueblo, Comanche, Pacific NW fishers. Devastated by disease + dispossession + war. Population fell from ~5-10M to under 250,000 by 1900.

nodes.label: Columbian Exchange
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Post-1492 exchange of plants, animals, diseases, and peoples between Americas and Afro-Eurasia. Potato + maize transformed European diets. Smallpox decimated Americans. American silver financed European trade with Asia (incl India textiles).
nodes.chapter_title: The Making of a Global World

nodes.label: Atlantic Slave Trade
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: ~12-15M Africans transported to Americas 16c-19c. Triangular trade: Europe manufactures→Africa; African captives→Americas; American sugar/cotton/tobacco→Europe. Largest forced migration in history.

nodes.label: Plantation Economy (Americas)
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Large agricultural estates producing sugar, tobacco, cotton, coffee for European markets. Relied on enslaved African labour after indigenous decline. Enriched colonial powers; fuelled slave trade; shaped racial + economic structures.

nodes.label: Disease + Indigenous Depopulation
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: European diseases (smallpox, measles, influenza, typhus) devastated Americas and Australia indigenous peoples. ~90% American indigenous population died within a century. Australian Aboriginal communities similarly decimated.

nodes.label: Civil Rebellions 1763-1856
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Bipin Chandra: "From 1763 to 1856, more than 40 major rebellions apart from hundreds of minor ones." Led by deposed rajas/nawabs, impoverished zamindars, landed poligars, ex-retainers. Mass base from rack-rented peasants + ruined artisans + demobilised soldiers. Suppressed piecemeal; established local traditions of resistance.

nodes.label: Sanyasi Rebellion (1763-1800)
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Bengal + Bihar. Displaced peasants + demobilised soldiers led by religious monks + dispossessed zamindars. Bankim Chandra Chatterjee's novel Anand Math (1882) set in this rebellion — source of Vande Mataram.

nodes.label: Chuar Uprising (1766-1816)
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Adivasi uprising covering 5 districts of Bengal + Bihar (Midnapore, Bankura, Jungle Mahal). Against new revenue demands + incursions on tribal land. Active 1766-72 and again 1795-1816.

nodes.label: Poligar Revolts (South India, 1790s-1800s)
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Landed military magnates (poligars) of Tamil Nadu, Malabar, coastal Andhra rebelled against EIC's revenue + dispossession policies. Especially Virapandya Kattabomman of Panchalankurichi (Tirunelveli) executed 1799. Parlekamedi 1813-14.

nodes.label: Velu Thampi Dalawa Revolt (1805)
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Dewan of Travancore Velu Thampi led heroic revolt 1805 against EIC. Published Kundara Proclamation calling Kerala to arms. Defeated; committed suicide to avoid capture. Publicly hanged post-mortem.

nodes.label: Paika Rebellion (Orissa, 1817)
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Buxi Jagabandhu led Paikas (traditional military retainers of Khordha Raja) against British revenue policies after annexation of Orissa 1803. Widespread Paika revolt seized Puri, Cuttack briefly before suppression 1817-18. Considered an important 'first war of independence' by Odia nationalists.

nodes.label: Bhil Uprisings (1818-1831)
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Khandesh/Maharashtra Bhil tribal community repeatedly rose against British administration + moneylenders 1818-31. Sevaram Savara 1823 a known leader. Finally pacified through revenue concessions + Bhil Corps raised by Outram 1825.

nodes.label: Kittur Uprising (Rani Chennamma, 1824)
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Rani Chennamma of Kittur (Karnataka) resisted British annexation under Doctrine of Lapse 1824 after her husband's death. Defeated British in first battle; captured and imprisoned. Early case of woman-led resistance. Chinnava (Sangolli Rayanna) continued guerrilla till executed 1831.

nodes.label: Kol Rebellion (1820-1837)
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Chhotanagpur Kol tribals rose against moneylenders + outsider (diku) settlers + British revenue administration. Leaders Buddho Bhagat, Joa Bhagat. Thousands massacred before British reimposed authority.

nodes.label: Ramosi Uprising (Maharashtra, 1826-29)
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Chittur Singh and Umaji Naik led Ramosi peasant hillmen against British revenue after Peshwa defeat 1818. Plundered British posts. Umaji Naik hanged 1832.

nodes.label: Wahabi Movement (1820s-1870s)
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Islamic revivalist movement led by Sayyid Ahmad Barelvi (1786-1831, d. battling Sikhs at Balakot). Drew on Shah Waliullah tradition. Primary anti-British thrust in Bengal + NWFP. Active through 1857 and beyond. Suppressed after 1870 Wahabi Trials.

nodes.label: Faraizi Movement (Bengal, 1818-1860s)
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Bengal Muslim peasant movement founded by Haji Shariatullah (1781-1840), expanded by son Dudu Miyan. Called for Islamic piety + opposed British landlord + indigo planter exploitation. Crystallised ryot resistance especially to zamindars + indigo planters.

nodes.label: Moplah Rebellions (Malabar)
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Series of 1830s-1920s uprisings of Mappila (Moplah) Muslim peasants in Malabar (Kerala) against Hindu Namboodiri landlords + British revenue. 22 outbreaks between 1836 and 1854. Culminated in major 1921 rebellion during Khilafat/Non-cooperation.

nodes.label: Tanjore (Thanjavur) Paintings
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Maratha Bhonsle rulers patronised 18c+. Painted on glass + wooden boards. Brilliant colours + heavy gold leaf + gemstones + cut-glass embellishments. Mostly smiling Krishna + Hindu deities. Zenith under Sarfoji Maharaj (r. 1798-1832) of Thanjavur — who was also a scholar + ruler under Subsidiary Alliance.

nodes.label: Mysore Paintings
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Wodeyar-era Mysore court patronage, continued under British. Theme: Hindu gods and goddesses. Distinctive gesso paste base (zinc oxide + Arabic gum) giving sheen; muted colours. Two or more figures with one dominant.

nodes.label: Bazaar Paintings (Bengal-Bihar)
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: European-influenced school in colonial Bengal + Bihar. Differed from Company school: took Greco-Roman (not Indian) influence — copied classical statues. Painted everyday Indian bazaars with European backgrounds; Indian courtesans dancing before British. Avoided multi-armed deities.

nodes.label: Portuguese Goa Architecture
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Iberian style + Baroque. Sé Cathedral Goa (1619) late-Gothic. Basilica of Bom Jesus Goa (1604) Baroque, houses St Francis Xavier's body. Diu Fort 1535 with St Paul's (1610), St Thomas + St Francis Churches. Church of St Anne Talaulim (1695).

nodes.label: French Pondicherry Architecture
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: French brought Cartesian grid urban planning. Pondicherry + Chandannagar organised on scientific grid. Anonymous architecture (simple facades). Coastal French towns: Mahe (Kerala), Karaikal (Tamil Nadu), Yanam (Andhra). Sacred Heart Church Puducherry.

nodes.label: European Arrival + Early Company Trading
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Portuguese arrival (Vasco da Gama 1498), establishment of trading posts by Dutch, French, English East India Companies (1600). Black Towns, Portuguese Goa architecture, early Bombay (1661 dowry) and Calcutta (1690 Job Charnock). Fort William 1757 on eve of Plassey marks transition to Company rule.

nodes.label: Company Ascendancy (Plassey→Charter Act)
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Plassey 1757 → Charter Act 1813. Clive, Warren Hastings (first Governor-General 1772), Lord Cornwallis (Permanent Settlement 1793), Wellesley's Subsidiary Alliance (1798). Anglo-Mysore wars (4, 1767-1799) vs Haidar Ali + Tipu Sultan. Anglo-Maratha wars 1 & 2 (1775-1805). Regulating Act 1773, Pitt's India Act 1784. Diwani of Bengal 1765 made EIC a fiscal power.

nodes.label: Company Paramountcy (1813→1856)
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Charter Act 1813 → Awadh annexation 1856. Dalhousie's Doctrine of Lapse (Satara, Jhansi, Nagpur, Awadh). Anglo-Sikh wars + Punjab annexation 1849. First Anglo-Afghan war 1839-42. Bentinck reforms (sati abolition 1829, English Ed Act 1835). General Service Enlistment Act 1856 triggers sepoy unrest.

nodes.label: Revolt of 1857
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Great Rising of 1857-58. Meerut → Delhi (11 May 1857). Rebels declare Bahadur Shah Zafar emperor. Major centres: Delhi, Kanpur (Nana Sahib + Tantia Tope), Lucknow (Begum Hazrat Mahal + Birjis Qadr), Jhansi (Rani Lakshmibai), Bihar (Kunwar Singh). Causes: Doctrine of Lapse, revenue pressure, greased cartridges, religious anxiety. Suppressed by mid-1858; Crown rule via Queen Victoria's Proclamation Nov 1858 ends Company era.

nodes.label: Colonial Agrarian Systems
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Three revenue systems: Permanent Settlement (Bengal 1793, Cornwallis + Shore), Ryotwari (Madras/Bombay, Munro + Read 1820), Mahalwari (NW Provinces, Holt Mackenzie 1822). Cash crops: indigo (Bengal ryoti/nij systems, Blue Mutiny 1859-60), opium (Bengal for China trade), cotton (Deccan). Fifth Report 1813. Forest Acts 1865 (Brandis), Criminal Tribes Act 1871. Paharias, Santhals, Jotedars as agrarian actors.

nodes.label: Colonial Industry + Deindustrialisation
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Deindustrialisation — decline of Indian textile trade (Dacca muslin ruined 1830s), wootz steel lost. Calico Act 1720 (British protectionism). EIC textile revenue 1770. First cotton mill Bombay 1854, first jute mill Rishra 1855. Managing agencies (Bird Heilgers, Andrew Yule). Triangular trade: India opium→China tea→Britain→India. Proto-industrialisation + handloom survival.

nodes.label: Colonial Cities + Infrastructure
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Presidency cities grow — Bombay (7 islands reclaimed by 1862, chawls 1860s, cotton mills), Calcutta (Fort William 1757, White/Black town segregation, Bengal Renaissance), Madras (Fort St George). Urban planning asserts colonial authority. De-urbanisation of old cities (Surat, Machilipatnam, Seringapatam). Hill stations (Shimla, Darjeeling). Railways-driven urbanisation from 1853.

nodes.label: Colonial Education + Orientalism
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Orientalist phase: Calcutta Madrasa 1781 (Hastings), Asiatic Society 1784 (William Jones), Benares Sanskrit College 1791, Serampore Mission press 1800. Francis Buchanan + Colin Mackenzie surveyed India. Anglicist turn: James Mill, Macaulay's Minute 1835, English Education Act 1835 (end of Oriental funding), Wood's Despatch 1854 founds universities (Calcutta/Bombay/Madras 1857). Pathshala system eroded.

nodes.label: Social Reform + Bengal Renaissance
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Bengal Renaissance + reform. Raja Rammohun Roy (d.1833) — Brahmo Sabha 1828/Samaj 1830, Sati abolition 1829, press freedom vs 1823 Press Regulations. Ishwarchandra Vidyasagar — Widow Remarriage Act 1856, girls' schools. Young Bengal + Derozio. Rashsundari Devi first woman's autobiography. Jyotirao + Savitribai Phule: first girls' school Pune 1848. Shanar breast cloth movement, dress reform.

nodes.label: Colonial Art + Painting + Architecture
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Portuguese Iberian architecture (Sé Cathedral Goa 1619, Basilica of Bom Jesus 1604). French Cartesian Pondicherry. British Indo-Gothic/Victorian style (Victoria Terminus Bombay 1878). Indo-Saracenic late-19c. Indian painting: Tanjore (Maratha Bhonsle patronage, Sarfoji Raja), Mysore (Wodeyar, gesso paste), Company paintings (Impey/Wellesley — Sewak Ram, Ishwari Prasad, Ghulam Ali Khan), Kalighat pat, Bazaar paintings, Raja Ravi Varma.

nodes.label: Indian Resistance (civil + tribal + peasant, pre-1857)
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Bipin Chandra: 40+ major rebellions 1763-1856. Sanyasi (1763-1800), Chuar (1766-1816), Poligar revolts (Kattabomman 1799), Velu Thampi Travancore 1805, Paika/Buxi Jagabandhu Orissa 1817, Bhil 1818-31, Kittur (Rani Chennamma 1824), Kol 1820-37, Ramosi (Umaji Naik 1826), Wahabi (Sayyid Ahmad Barelvi), Faraizi (Haji Shariatullah Bengal), Moplah (Malabar 1836+), Santhal Hool (Sidhu-Kanhu 1855-56), Indigo Rebellion 1859-60.

nodes.label: Industrial Revolution + Capitalism (Britain + global)
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Britain's Industrial Revolution from 1760. Agricultural Revolution + Enclosure Acts freed labour. Inventions: spinning jenny (Hargreaves 1764), water frame (Arkwright 1769), steam engine (Watt 1769), factory system (Cromford 1771). Adam Smith's Wealth of Nations 1776. Coal + iron (Darby's coke-smelting, Cort's puddling). Railways from Stephenson 1829. Luddites 1811, Trade Unions legalised 1824, Chartists. Urbanisation of Manchester, London 1M→6.5M. Feeds Indian deindustrialisation.

nodes.label: French Revolution + European Nationalism
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Rousseau's Social Contract 1762, American Revolution 1776 backdrop. French Revolution 1789 — Estates General, Bastille, Declaration of Rights of Man, Jacobins + Robespierre, Reign of Terror 1793-94. Napoleon 1804 + Civil Code. Congress of Vienna 1815 restores monarchies. Romantic nationalism (Grimm, Mazzini's Young Italy 1831). Greek Independence 1832, 1848 Revolutions. Set stage for Bismarck + Italian unification (era 8).

nodes.label: Settler Colonialism (Americas + Australia)
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Columbus 1492 → Atlantic slave trade + plantation economy in Americas. Disease kills 90% of Americans. US westward expansion (Appalachian 1800 → Mississippi → Great Plains), Manifest Destiny, Trail of Tears 1830, Indian Removal Act, Gold Rush 1848, wheat bread basket. Australia 1788 — terra nullius, Aboriginal dispossession, wool industry, gold rushes. Stolen Generations (era 8). Maasai East Africa — Anglo-German split 1885.

nodes.label: East Asia (Qing China + Tokugawa/Meiji Japan)
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: China: Qing Dynasty decline. Opium Wars (1839-42 + 1856-60), Treaty of Nanking 1842 cedes Hong Kong + 5 treaty ports. Commissioner Lin Zexu's 1839 confiscation. Taiping Rebellion 1850-64 (Hong Xiuquan, 20-30M deaths). Japan: Tokugawa sakoku isolation → Commodore Perry 1853 forces opening → Meiji Restoration 1868 (fukoku kyohei) launches state-led industrialisation. Samurai transformation.
